questions.stem: A circular resale unit has near-zero production cost but still costs to run. Which statement is most precise?

options.A: Cost becomes irrelevant because circularity eliminates rivalry and substitutes
options.B: Cost rises above new production because used goods require mandatory depreciation
options.C: Variable production cost can be near zero, but handling and platform costs still matter
options.D: Total cost is zero, so resale units must always be pure profit regardless of scale

questions.explanation: Resale avoids manufacturing cost, but processing, authentication, shipping, and customer service still create costs. The wedge depends on net costs and capture.

questions.stem: A company claims 'sustainability' with no third-party verification. In signaling terms, what is missing?

options.A: A temporary discount that makes mimicry unattractive for high-quality firms
options.B: A credible cost that makes mimicry unprofitable for low-commitment firms
options.C: A capacity expansion that makes mimicry easy for high-quality entrants
options.D: A lobbying coalition that makes mimicry illegal for low-quality rivals

questions.explanation: Verification creates a real cost and constraint. Without it, sustainability claims become cheap talk that competitors can mimic without changing operations.

questions.stem: A competitor can copy Patagonia's ads but not its repair network. Which concept best explains the defensibility?

options.A: The hard-to-copy capability is the target segment itself, which cannot be reached by rivals
options.B: The hard-to-copy capability is the shortness of the ad text, which is inherently rare
options.C: The hard-to-copy capability is the system of routines and infrastructure, not the slogan
options.D: The hard-to-copy capability is the font and design language, which is protected by copyright

questions.explanation: Advantage often rests on complex systems: logistics, service networks, training, and culture. Messaging is easy to imitate; capability systems are not.

questions.stem: A firm claims 'purpose eliminates trade-offs.' What is the most accurate response?

options.A: Purpose clarifies priorities, but trade-offs remain and must be managed explicitly
options.B: Purpose eliminates trade-offs because customers always pay more for moral products
options.C: Purpose eliminates trade-offs because regulation protects mission firms from rivalry
options.D: Purpose eliminates trade-offs because cost declines automatically with authenticity

questions.explanation: Strategy is about choices under constraints. Purpose can guide those choices, but it does not remove economic trade-offs in price, cost, and scope.

questions.stem: A firm increases durability. Which pattern best preserves advantage rather than eroding it?

options.A: Lower cost via lower quality, then capture via higher returns and warranty claims
options.B: Lower value via fewer purchases, then capture via commoditised accessories sales
options.C: Increase value via quality and trust, then capture via premium pricing and services
options.D: Increase cost via quality, then capture via discounts and higher replacement rates

questions.explanation: Durability can raise willingness to pay and reduce leakage. To preserve capture, firms often combine premium pricing with services, subscriptions, or resale economics.

questions.stem: A firm prices below cost to gain share. Which statement is most correct in surplus terms?

options.A: Consumer surplus must fall because low price signals low quality to all buyers
options.B: Consumer surplus can increase while producer surplus turns negative at the firm level
options.C: Producer surplus must rise because higher share always improves bargaining power
options.D: Both surpluses must rise because penetration pricing creates network effects always

questions.explanation: Low prices can raise customer surplus. But if price is below cost, the firm is destroying producer surplus and relying on future cost declines or future pricing power.

questions.stem: A firm reports record revenue but shrinking wedge per unit. What is the best inference?

options.A: Revenue guarantees advantage because it implies the market is expanding
options.B: Revenue implies lower cost because scale always reduces variable cost immediately
options.C: Revenue implies higher value because familiarity always increases willingness to pay
options.D: Volume can mask eroding advantage; unit wedge is central for sustainability

questions.explanation: Topline can grow while per-unit economics deteriorate. Sustainable advantage requires maintaining or widening the wedge relative to rivals, not only growing volume.

questions.stem: A founder claims 'our ESG brand is our moat.' Which evidence best supports that claim in wedge terms?

options.A: Higher charitable donations as a share of revenue compared with rivals
options.B: Higher employee headcount growth compared with rivals in a single quarter
options.C: Higher willingness to pay and retention at similar cost levels compared with rivals
options.D: Higher social media mentions and influencer content compared with rivals

questions.explanation: A brand moat should show up as sustained pricing power and loyalty. Those effects widen the wedge and improve long-run capture.

questions.stem: A founder says: 'High costs mean no competitive advantage.' Which correction is conceptually tight?

options.A: Advantage depends on revenue, so cost is irrelevant when volume is large
options.B: Advantage depends on share, so cost is secondary to market dominance
options.C: Advantage depends on V-C, so cost can be high if value rises more
options.D: Advantage depends on ROE, so cost matters only when equity is growing

questions.explanation: Competitive advantage is about creating and capturing more economic value than rivals. High cost can still be consistent with advantage if willingness to pay rises even more.

questions.stem: A founder says: 'Maximise consumer surplus and advantage follows.' What is the sharpest critique?

options.A: Consumer surplus implies low prices, which always forces costs down through scale
options.B: Consumer surplus can be high while capture is low; pricing and cost discipline still matter
options.C: Consumer surplus equals producer surplus, so maximising either always yields profit
options.D: Consumer surplus is unobservable, so strategy cannot use it for decisions at all

questions.explanation: A firm can delight customers yet lose money if it cannot capture value. Sustainable advantage requires both creating value and capturing enough of it.

questions.stem: A luxury brand donates heavily but sells mediocre products. What is the most wedge-consistent outcome?

options.A: Donations ensure loyalty, so willingness to pay rises even if quality is inconsistent
options.B: Donations may not offset weak value delivery, so willingness to pay and retention fall
options.C: Donations reduce supplier power directly, so costs fall enough to restore value
options.D: Donations eliminate substitutes because activism makes rivals morally unacceptable

questions.explanation: If product performance is weak, the core value proposition fails. Social spending cannot reliably compensate for low quality when customers experience defects.

questions.stem: A mission-led D2C brand polarises customers and loses some buyers. Which wedge statement is most defensible?

options.A: Value rises only when activism produces subsidies rather than loyalty effects
options.B: Value is fixed by category norms so only cost can change through purpose
options.C: Value must fall whenever any segment exits because willingness is an average
options.D: Value can rise for a smaller segment that has higher willingness to pay

questions.explanation: Differentiation may trade breadth for depth. Losing low-WTP customers can still increase average realised value if the remaining segment pays more and stays longer.

questions.stem: A public company boosts EPS via buybacks without changing product economics. Which statement is most correct?

options.A: Buybacks directly reduce supplier power because investors threaten supplier contracts
options.B: Buybacks directly lower substitutes because rivals cannot match capital return policies
options.C: Share count changes can lift per-share metrics even if the customer-level wedge is unchanged
options.D: Buybacks directly raise willingness to pay because customers value financial discipline

questions.explanation: Financial policy can improve per-share outcomes without improving competitive advantage. The wedge is still determined by value created and captured in the product market.

questions.stem: A quick-commerce startup grows orders by heavy coupons while unit economics stay negative. In wedge terms, what is most accurate?

options.A: Both surpluses fall because coupons always reduce perceived value in markets
options.B: Consumer surplus rises, but producer surplus stays negative because C exceeds P
options.C: Both surpluses rise because scale guarantees falling variable costs immediately
options.D: Producer surplus rises, but consumer surplus stays negative because P exceeds V

questions.explanation: Subsidies can create high consumer surplus (V-P) while the firm loses money if cost exceeds price (C>P). That is not sustainable advantage unless costs fall or capture improves.

questions.stem: A rival copies Patagonia messaging but delivers inconsistent quality. The most likely strategic outcome is:

options.A: The mimic reduces rivalry, so both firms benefit through tacit price coordination
options.B: The mimic increases rarity, so Patagonia advantage automatically becomes stronger
options.C: The messaging alone creates advantage, so quality becomes strategically secondary
options.D: The positioning-operations mismatch erodes credibility, shrinking relative willingness to pay

questions.explanation: Differentiation requires internal consistency. If execution contradicts claims, credibility collapses and willingness to pay declines, harming the wedge.

questions.stem: A startup frames purpose as advantage but has no distinctive capabilities. What is the best diagnosis?

options.A: Intent reduces buyer power, so costs and differentiation no longer matter
options.B: Intent substitutes for execution, so operations can be average safely
options.C: Intent automatically signals quality, so advantage follows unless regulated
options.D: Intent without hard-to-copy routines becomes rhetoric and does not widen the wedge

questions.explanation: Purpose becomes strategic when embedded in processes, products, and governance that rivals cannot easily imitate. Otherwise it remains branding.

questions.stem: A student claims: 'Economic value equals accounting profit.' Which distinction is most correct?

options.A: Economic value is V-C per unit; accounting profit is realised P minus accounting cost
options.B: Economic value is EPS; accounting profit is customer satisfaction and loyalty
options.C: Economic value is book value; accounting profit is market value minus book value
options.D: Economic value is revenue growth; accounting profit is market capitalisation growth

questions.explanation: Economic value (the wedge) is a conceptual measure of value created, while accounting profit reflects realised revenues minus recorded costs over a period.

questions.stem: A sustainability startup runs 'buy less' messaging but then runs weekly deep discounts. What is the best signaling diagnosis?

options.A: The message becomes stronger, since discounts prove confidence in product quality
options.B: The message becomes exclusive, since discounts reduce buyer power through loyalty
options.C: The message becomes cheap talk, weakening credibility and shrinking value uplift
options.D: The message becomes irrelevant, since willingness to pay is fixed by category norms

questions.explanation: Signals work when they are costly and consistent. Frequent discounting can undermine the credibility of restraint, weakening the trust-based willingness-to-pay effect.

questions.stem: NVIDIA claims new chips reduce energy per unit compute for cloud customers. Which statement best applies V-C logic for the buyer?

options.A: Buyer cost per output falls, expanding their wedge even at similar pricing
options.B: Buyer price must rise because efficiency always triggers premium pricing
options.C: Buyer value falls because efficiency lowers perceived performance prestige
options.D: Buyer costs rise because integration friction dominates all efficiency gains

questions.explanation: If performance per watt improves, the buyer's effective cost of delivering compute can fall. That expands the buyer's V-C even if supplier pricing is unchanged.

questions.stem: Patagonia says "Dont buy this jacket" and still sells more later. Which wedge mechanism best fits?

options.A: It forces supplier concessions that reduce unit cost through scale
options.B: It signals costly restraint that raises trust and willingness to pay
options.C: It creates price discrimination by splitting buyers into many micro tiers
options.D: It eliminates substitutes by lobbying for stricter product regulations

questions.explanation: A credible self-limiting message works as costly signaling. It can raise willingness to pay by strengthening authenticity and trust, widening V-C without requiring lower cost.

questions.stem: Patagonia's Worn Wear revenue is small relative to total sales, yet strategic. Which is the best reason?

options.A: It is small, so it must be loss-making and therefore reduces the wedge automatically
options.B: It is small, so it cannot matter strategically and should be treated as philanthropy
options.C: It reinforces credibility and adds service capture, influencing the core business economics
options.D: It is small, so it can be ignored because it cannot influence customer loyalty at all

questions.explanation: Even small lines can shape brand meaning, retention, and pricing power. They can also reduce returns and warranty leakage, strengthening the economics of the main product.

questions.stem: Patagonia's repair and resale (Worn Wear) most plausibly strengthens advantage by which combined effect?

options.A: It adds service capture while reinforcing durability claims, lifting lifetime value
options.B: It commoditises the brand because repair services remove differentiation in apparel
options.C: It prevents cannibalisation because used goods create zero incremental transactions
options.D: It raises switching costs through proprietary repair patents and exclusive parts

questions.explanation: Repairs and resale can reinforce the brand promise (raising V) and create additional revenue streams (improving capture), supporting a stronger lifetime wedge.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best explains why a mission governance commitment can raise long-run economic value?

options.A: It strengthens trust-based intangibles that support willingness to pay over time
options.B: It forces austerity that lowers cost mechanically through reduced reinvestment
options.C: It guarantees monopoly by placing the firm under legal protection from entry
options.D: It eliminates trade-offs by allowing low prices and high quality simultaneously

questions.explanation: Commitment devices can make purpose credible, strengthening reputation and loyalty. Those intangibles can widen V-C and improve resilience across cycles.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures Porter-Kramer 'shared value' rather than generic CSR?

options.A: Competitiveness gains that also measurably improve social conditions in the ecosystem
options.B: Compliance with regulation even when it reduces competitiveness and productivity
options.C: Brand campaigns that signal virtue without operational change or measurement
options.D: Donations after profits, regardless of whether the action changes the value chain

questions.explanation: Shared value links social improvement to the firm's competitive position through products, value chain productivity, or cluster development, not post-profit philanthropy.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes 'shareholder return' from 'competitive advantage'?

options.A: Returns rise only when substitutes disappear and rivalry becomes negligible
options.B: Returns rise only when customer willingness to pay rises sharply above rivals
options.C: Returns rise only when supplier power falls and input prices drop permanently
options.D: Returns can rise via capital policy even when customer-level V-C is unchanged

questions.explanation: Shareholder returns can be influenced by payout policy, leverage, and market sentiment. Competitive advantage is rooted in product-market economics and relative wedge.

questions.stem: A CFO evaluates repair strategy only by quarterly new unit growth. Best critique?

options.A: It ignores service margin, retention, reduced returns, and lifetime cash flow effects
options.B: It ignores price elasticity, which becomes irrelevant once brand trust is high enough
options.C: It ignores market cap, which is the only valid measure of performance for strategy
options.D: It ignores ESG ratings, which automatically predict accounting profitability each year

questions.explanation: Circular initiatives affect multiple cash and margin drivers. Evaluating only new unit sales misses where value is created and captured.

questions.stem: A CFO says: 'High current ratio proves low liquidity risk.' Which correction is best?

options.A: Inventory can inflate current assets; quick ratio tests near-cash solvency more directly
options.B: Current ratio measures market cap, so it reflects investor optimism only
options.C: Current ratio ignores liabilities, so it cannot measure liquidity risk in any way
options.D: Current ratio equals profit margin, so it measures demand rather than solvency

questions.explanation: A firm can look liquid on current ratio yet be vulnerable if assets are slow-moving inventory. Quick ratio is stricter because it focuses on cash-like assets.

questions.stem: A circular model reduces new production but increases service volume. Which cost category most plausibly changes first?

options.A: Interest rises because resale requires mandatory long-term debt issuance under GAAP rules
options.B: Depreciation declines because resale converts fixed assets into inventory on balance sheet
options.C: Variable production and return-handling costs per customer served can decline over time
options.D: Tax rises because resale eliminates all deductions from repair expenses permanently

questions.explanation: Less new production and fewer returns can reduce variable cost and leakage. Depreciation, interest, and tax effects depend on financing and accounting specifics, not circularity alone.

questions.stem: A circular program reduces returns and improves retention but lowers this-quarter revenue. What is the best course metric response?

options.A: Raise discounts to restore quarterly revenue even if it reduces trust and margins
options.B: Use a multi-period score that tracks lifetime margin and leakage, not one-quarter revenue only
options.C: Shift all reporting to social media metrics because financial measures lag too much
options.D: Stop the program because revenue is the only valid measure of strategy performance

questions.explanation: Quarterly revenue can be noisy. The right evaluation should include retention, service margins, return costs, and lifetime profitability to test whether the wedge is improving.

questions.stem: A circular resale unit avoids manufacturing cost but still uses labour and logistics. Which statement is most precise?

options.A: Cost is irrelevant because circularity eliminates rivalry and substitutes permanently
options.B: Cost exceeds new production because used goods require mandatory depreciation expense
options.C: Total cost becomes zero, so resale units must always be pure profit at any scale
options.D: Manufacturing cost can be near zero, but processing and fulfilment costs still matter

questions.explanation: Resale avoids production cost but not operations cost. Sorting, authentication, shipping, and customer service still determine the net cost base.

questions.stem: A company improves quick ratio by delaying supplier payments. Best classification?

options.A: A working-capital tactic that improves optics but may harm supplier relations and resilience
options.B: A shared-value innovation that increases cluster productivity and margins automatically
options.C: A differentiation move that raises willingness to pay through costly signaling alone
options.D: A capability build that increases inimitability through learning routines immediately

questions.explanation: Stretching payables can lift reported liquidity, but it can also create operational fragility and damage supplier trust. It is not inherently value creating.

questions.stem: A consumer brand has a large gap between current and quick ratios. Which diagnosis best fits?

options.A: Capital is tied up in inventory, creating liquidity risk if demand shifts suddenly
options.B: Receivables dominate assets, so the firm faces immediate default risk always
options.C: Cash is abundant relative to liabilities, so the firm faces minimal solvency risk
options.D: Payables dominate liabilities, so the firm must be overpaying suppliers rapidly

questions.explanation: A big gap suggests inventory-heavy current assets. That can be normal in apparel, but it creates risk when trends or demand conditions change.

questions.stem: A firm factors receivables (sells them at a discount) to raise cash. All else equal, what is the most likely immediate ratio effect?

options.A: Quick ratio may dip slightly due to the discount, even though cash availability improves
options.B: Both ratios become meaningless because receivables are no longer an accounting category
options.C: Current ratio rises sharply because receivables move out of current assets entirely
options.D: Quick ratio rises sharply because factoring converts receivables into revenue

questions.explanation: Factoring swaps receivables for cash but typically at a discount. Since both are in quick assets, the ratio may fall slightly, while the quality of liquidity improves.

questions.stem: A firm funds a circular initiative by raising equity, boosting current ratio. Best interpretation?

options.A: Financing proves monopoly because investors fund only firms with protected market power
options.B: Financing proves advantage because cash is the same as differentiation in consumer markets
options.C: Financing improves solvency, but competitive advantage still depends on operating wedge and capture
options.D: Financing proves cost leadership because new equity automatically lowers supplier prices

questions.explanation: Capital raises can fix liquidity. But advantage is driven by product-market economics: willingness to pay, cost position, and ability to capture value sustainably.

questions.stem: A firm improves current ratio by stockpiling inventory ahead of a season. What is the most careful view?

options.A: Current ratio improves and leverage falls because inventory counts as equity under GAAP
options.B: Current ratio improves and liquidity improves because inventory is always near cash
options.C: Current ratio may improve while actual liquidity worsens if stock is slow moving
options.D: Current ratio improves and quick ratio improves because inventory raises both equally

questions.explanation: Inventory increases current assets but may not be easily convertible to cash. Liquidity should be tested with quick ratio and cash conversion analysis.

questions.stem: A firm improves quick ratio by raising short-term debt and holding cash. Most accurate interpretation?

options.A: Liquidity optics improve and risk falls because debt always lowers the cost of capital
options.B: Liquidity optics may improve, but refinancing risk rises; underlying wedge is unchanged
options.C: Liquidity optics improve and rivalry falls because debt signals strength to competitors
options.D: Liquidity optics improve and value rises because cash holdings raise willingness to pay

questions.explanation: Borrowing to hold cash can lift the quick ratio but increases leverage and refinancing risk. It does not automatically improve competitiveness or unit economics.

questions.stem: A firm reports strong cash flows after cutting warranty payouts by denying claims. What is the best risk framing?

options.A: Short-run cash proves cost leadership because denying claims reduces supplier power
options.B: Short-run cash proves advantage because customers do not notice warranty policy shifts
options.C: Short-run cash proves monopoly because only monopolists can change warranty terms
options.D: Short-run cash can improve while trust erodes, reducing willingness to pay and retention later

questions.explanation: Liquidity gains achieved by harming the promise can destroy the intangible trust asset. Over time that can shrink value and raise churn, harming the wedge.

questions.stem: A firm tracks 'number of repairs completed' as its primary KPI. What is the deepest critique?

options.A: Counts equal market valuation because investors price repair counts directly each quarter
options.B: Counts equal liquidity because repairs are near-cash and can replace cash holdings
options.C: Counts are activity, not outcome; link to retention, margins, and wedge measures is needed
options.D: Counts guarantee advantage automatically; outcomes are secondary for mission firms

questions.explanation: Activity metrics can be misleading. Strategy needs outcome metrics: net margin, returns reduction, repeat rate, and lifetime value relative to cost.

questions.stem: A founder claims: 'Liquidity ratios are a competitive advantage.' What is the best correction?

options.A: Ratios are outcomes; advantage comes from capabilities that shape cash conversion and wedge
options.B: Ratios equal economic value; strategy is simply maximising ratio targets directly
options.C: Ratios equal customer trust; liquidity is created by brand love without operations
options.D: Ratios are inputs; advantage is created by manipulating balance sheet optics deliberately

questions.explanation: Liquidity is important, but it reflects operational choices (inventory policy, receivables, payables). Advantage is created by capabilities that improve those economics sustainably.

questions.stem: A founder says: 'Circular models always raise profits.' What is the strongest correction?

options.A: They always reduce costs; circular operations are cheaper by definition in every industry
options.B: They always raise willingness to pay; circularity mechanically increases value for all buyers
options.C: They can cannibalise new sales; profitability depends on pricing, costs, and capture design
options.D: They never cannibalise new sales; circular demand is always purely incremental volume

questions.explanation: Circularity can create value but also reduce new unit sales. Whether profits rise depends on how services are priced, operational costs, and whether loyalty offsets cannibalisation.

questions.stem: A growth startup scales revenue fast but burns cash; current ratio worsens. Best interpretation?

options.A: Worsening ratio proves demand is falling because customers have stopped paying entirely
options.B: Solvency is irrelevant because capital markets always refinance any fast-growing firm
options.C: Solvency risk rises even if demand is real; dependence on external financing increases
options.D: Worsening ratio proves costs are falling because suppliers are subsidising operations

questions.explanation: Burn can outpace growth, creating liquidity risk. Even strong growth can be fragile if the firm must continually raise capital to meet short-term obligations.

questions.stem: A repair-first strategy can reduce returns but also depress quarterly new-unit sales. What is the most disciplined conclusion?

options.A: Short-run revenue dip proves the strategy is wrong and must be reversed immediately
options.B: Short-run revenue can dip while long-run wedge expands through loyalty and lower leakage
options.C: Short-run revenue dip proves the firm has shifted to cost leadership and must discount more
options.D: Short-run revenue dip proves the firm is losing differentiation irreversibly in the category

questions.explanation: Circularity can shift value capture from new sales to services and retention. Quarter-to-quarter revenue may fall even if lifetime economics improve.

questions.stem: A retailer's current ratio rises while its quick ratio falls. What is the most plausible cause?

options.A: Inventory builds faster than payables, raising current assets but not quick assets
options.B: Receivables shrink faster than cash, lowering both ratios simultaneously
options.C: Cash builds faster than receivables, raising both ratios in the same direction
options.D: Liabilities fall faster than assets, raising quick ratio more than current

questions.explanation: Current ratio includes inventory, while quick ratio excludes it. If inventory accumulates, current ratio can improve even as near-cash liquidity deteriorates.

questions.stem: A subscription 'care plan' for repairs pulls which cash-flow lever most directly?

options.A: It eliminates receivables entirely, making current ratio mathematically undefined
options.B: It pushes cash backward via deferred revenue, increasing short-run liquidity risk
options.C: It pulls cash forward via recurring payments, reducing seasonal working-capital pressure
options.D: It eliminates payables entirely, making quick ratio mathematically undefined

questions.explanation: Subscriptions shift cash timing by collecting earlier and more predictably. That can reduce reliance on inventory financing and improve solvency stability.

questions.stem: An apparel firm takes an inventory write-down. Immediate ratio effect, all else equal?

options.A: Current ratio likely falls; quick ratio is mostly unchanged if only inventory is reduced
options.B: Current ratio rises; quick ratio rises because inventory is removed from assets
options.C: Current ratio is unchanged; quick ratio rises because COGS falls immediately
options.D: Current ratio rises; quick ratio is unchanged because liabilities revalue downward

questions.explanation: A write-down reduces inventory and therefore current assets, lowering the current ratio. Quick ratio excludes inventory, so it changes little unless cash or receivables move.

questions.stem: If inventory write downs become frequent in a category, what is the most plausible strategic signal?

options.A: Demand is uncertain or fashion risk is high, so inventory management capability matters more
options.B: Demand is stable, so inventory write downs prove the firm is intentionally donating value
options.C: Demand is rising, so inventory write downs prove the firm is underpricing systematically
options.D: Demand is irrelevant, so inventory write downs are only tax optimization and not strategic

questions.explanation: Repeated write-downs often reflect forecasting errors and volatile demand. Strong inventory and supply-chain capabilities can become a differentiator in such markets.

questions.stem: Patagonia reports Worn Wear revenue is small versus total revenue. Why can it still matter financially?

options.A: It is small, so it can only matter if it eliminates substitutes through regulation
options.B: It is small, so it must be loss making and therefore reduces economic value automatically
options.C: It reinforces brand trust and reduces leakage, which can support premium pricing and retention
options.D: It is small, so it cannot change any accounting driver and should be ignored entirely

questions.explanation: Small lines can shift overall economics by shaping willingness to pay and reducing return costs. They may also create profitable service margins and increase customer lifetime value.

questions.stem: When current ratio looks healthy but quick ratio is weak, what is the core risk?

options.A: Liquidity is guaranteed because suppliers must extend credit to inventory-heavy firms
options.B: Liquidity depends on selling inventory; shocks can create cash crunch despite strong optics
options.C: Liquidity is guaranteed because inventory can always be sold at book value quickly
options.D: Liquidity is irrelevant because mission firms can always access donations to pay bills

questions.explanation: Inventory may be illiquid during demand shocks. A weak quick ratio means the firm may struggle to meet near-term obligations without selling stock at discounts.

questions.stem: Which metric is most sensitive to inventory changes, given current vs quick ratio definitions?

options.A: Both ratios are identical; inventory affects neither under standard accounting
options.B: Quick ratio is more sensitive; current ratio is less sensitive because it includes inventory
options.C: Neither ratio is meaningful; inventory does not appear on the balance sheet in practice
options.D: Current ratio is more sensitive; quick ratio is less sensitive because it excludes inventory

questions.explanation: Inventory sits in current assets, so it directly affects the current ratio. Quick ratio removes inventory to focus on cash-like liquidity.

questions.stem: Which statement best links liquidity to strategy without confusing them?

options.A: Strong liquidity directly removes substitutes because substitutes cannot access capital markets
options.B: Strong liquidity can fund investments, but it does not itself create competitive advantage
options.C: Strong liquidity directly raises willingness to pay because customers prefer cash-rich firms
options.D: Strong liquidity directly lowers supplier power because suppliers fear cash hoarding behaviour

questions.explanation: Liquidity is a resource that can enable strategic moves. But advantage comes from product-market economics and hard-to-copy capabilities, not ratios alone.

questions.stem: A CEO tries to raise stock price only by cutting training budgets. In this syllabus logic, what is the main risk?

options.A: Training cuts raise willingness to pay because customers prefer understaffed service models
options.B: Training cuts raise quick ratio because employees are treated as current assets
options.C: Training cuts raise inimitability because fewer skills make culture more unique by default
options.D: Short-run profit may rise while capability intangibles erode, harming long-run value creation

questions.explanation: Cuts can boost earnings temporarily, but they can degrade service quality and execution capability. Markets may later revise expectations downward.

questions.stem: A biotech startup with few tangibles has a large valuation. In this module, the best explanation is:

options.A: The firm must be manipulating accounts because valuation requires large tangible assets
options.B: The firm must be over-inventoried because valuation reflects stockpiled physical goods
options.C: The firm must be colluding because high valuation implies illegal monopoly behaviour
options.D: Expected future cash flows from IP and pipeline options drive value beyond book assets

questions.explanation: Valuation can be dominated by growth options and intellectual property. These are often not fully represented on the balance sheet, especially pre-profit firms.

questions.stem: A company announces a massive buyback; product quality and retention are slipping. Under this module, what is the cleanest concern?

options.A: Buybacks always fix retention because investors become loyal customers after repurchases
options.B: Buybacks reduce supplier power because suppliers fear share count reduction trends
options.C: Buybacks remove substitutes because rivals cannot match payout policies in any market
options.D: Per-share optics can improve while capability and brand intangibles erode, harming long-run value

questions.explanation: Buybacks affect capital allocation and per-share metrics. They do not automatically repair product-market fundamentals, and underinvestment can weaken long-run cash flows.

questions.stem: A company has a high market-to-book ratio. In this module, what is the most defensible first explanation?

options.A: Investors have violated equilibrium because market must equal book for all listed firms
options.B: Investors assume the firm is highly leveraged because high ratios require high debt
options.C: Investors attribute significant value to intangibles and growth options not on the balance sheet
options.D: Investors anticipate a dividend increase because high ratios always precede payouts

questions.explanation: Book value records historical costs and capitalised items. Market value reflects forward-looking expectations, including brand, IP, networks, and growth options.

questions.stem: A company has high market-to-book because it has large goodwill after acquisitions. What is the best caution?

options.A: Goodwill eliminates risk because it is a tangible asset that can be sold for cash anytime
options.B: Goodwill guarantees superior capability, so a high ratio is always evidence of advantage
options.C: Market-to-book can be high for different reasons; test whether competitive intangibles actually drive cash flows
options.D: Goodwill reduces costs mechanically because accounting amortisation lowers supplier prices

questions.explanation: A high ratio can reflect real capability expectations or accounting artifacts like goodwill. Strategic diagnosis should look for pricing power, retention, and productivity evidence.

questions.stem: A company has strong brand awareness but churn is high and reviews worsen. Best intangible diagnosis?

options.A: Awareness guarantees market power, so substitutes cannot discipline the firm
options.B: Awareness exists, but brand meaning is decaying; intangible value is fragile and reversible
options.C: Awareness equals book value, so reviews cannot influence intangible assets at all
options.D: Awareness proves inimitability, so churn is irrelevant to competitive advantage

questions.explanation: Brand is not just recall; it is meaning and trust. High churn and deteriorating reviews signal that the intangible is weakening and future cash flows may fall.

questions.stem: A company spends heavily to rebuild trust after a crisis; accounting profit falls. What is the most coherent valuation implication?

options.A: If actions credibly restore loyalty and reduce churn risk, market value may recover before profits do
options.B: If profit falls today, market value must fall permanently because markets cannot price recovery
options.C: If profit falls today, book value must rise because expenses increase asset values directly
options.D: If profit falls today, dividends must rise because firms compensate investors automatically

questions.explanation: Valuation can move on expectations. If the market believes trust will recover and future cash flows will normalise, price can recover earlier than accounting results.

questions.stem: A firm says 'we are undervalued because our book value is high.' What is the sharpest issue?

options.A: High book value does not guarantee future cash flows; value depends on expected economics and risk
options.B: High book value guarantees low cost, so willingness to pay must rise automatically
options.C: High book value guarantees liquidity, so price must equal book within one quarter
options.D: High book value guarantees monopoly, so the market must be mispricing by definition

questions.explanation: Book value is historical and may reflect assets that do not generate attractive returns. Markets focus on expected future cash flows relative to risk.

questions.stem: A firm with few tangibles but high valuation faces a failed product trial. What is the most likely valuation driver?

options.A: Expected future cash flows from growth options collapse, so market value can drop sharply
options.B: Liquidity collapses to zero because valuation and cash balance are the same thing
options.C: Book value collapses to zero because accounting immediately writes off all assets
options.D: Share count collapses to zero because exchanges delist firms automatically on bad news

questions.explanation: Valuation for option-like firms depends on future success probabilities. Bad news can drastically reduce expected cash flows even if accounting assets change slowly.

questions.stem: A firm's brand is strong and competitors copy messaging easily. What sustains the intangible advantage?

options.A: Higher inventory levels that automatically create scarcity and willingness to pay
options.B: Consistent operational delivery that makes the claim credible and hard to imitate at scale
options.C: A larger advertising budget that prevents imitation because smaller rivals cannot speak
options.D: Shorter slogans that signal sophistication because brevity is inherently rare

questions.explanation: Messaging is easy to copy. Advantage comes from the system behind the claim: quality control, service routines, governance, and culture that sustain credibility.

questions.stem: A firm's market value rises after a large R&D expense that lowers accounting profit. Which interpretation best fits valuation logic?

options.A: Markets price expected future cash flows from capability building, not only current profit
options.B: Markets price only dividends, so the rise must reflect an immediate payout increase
options.C: Markets price only book assets, so the rise must reflect new tangible factories
options.D: Markets price only current earnings, so any rise must be an irrational mispricing

questions.explanation: If investors believe the R&D creates valuable intangibles, they may revise expectations upward. Accounting profit can fall today while expected future cash flows rise.

questions.stem: A founder insists 'intangibles are vague and should be ignored.' Which response is most defensible?

options.A: They cannot be linked to cash flows, so strategy should focus only on tangible assets
options.B: They can be measured indirectly through pricing power, churn, adoption risk, and retention trends
options.C: They equal goodwill only, so they appear only after acquisitions and never before
options.D: They are illegal because intangibles cannot be audited and therefore cannot be discussed

questions.explanation: Intangibles are not mystical; they show up in behaviour and economics. Firms can track them with leading indicators and wedge-linked metrics.

questions.stem: A mission firm makes governance commitments that constrain extraction. Which intangible is most directly strengthened?

options.A: Fixed asset collateral base, lowering interest rates mechanically without operations change
options.B: Credible commitment to mission, reinforcing authenticity, trust, and employee alignment
options.C: Inventory turnover, lowering working capital without any supply chain investment
options.D: Tax shields, raising depreciation and lowering effective tax rate permanently

questions.explanation: Commitment devices can increase credibility. That can support willingness to pay, retention, and talent attraction, which matter for long-run cash flows.

questions.stem: A platform launches a credible new capability that will scale next year; profits today are unchanged. Which is most likely to move first?

options.A: Market value may rise now because expected future cash flows and growth options improve
options.B: Book value rises now because accounting immediately capitalises all new capabilities
options.C: Depreciation rises now because capabilities are always recorded as tangible equipment
options.D: Liquidity ratio rises now because customer trust instantly becomes cash on the balance sheet

questions.explanation: When information shifts expectations, valuation can move before accounting profit. This is especially true for intangible-heavy capability expansions.

questions.stem: A scandal hits a consumer platform and market value falls even though factories and servers remain. Best explanation?

options.A: Inventory disappears immediately, so liquidity ratios must mechanically fall to zero
options.B: Share count changes automatically after scandals, so market cap must fall regardless of price
options.C: Tangible assets become unusable overnight, so the physical value must be near zero
options.D: Trust and reputation intangibles collapse, lowering expected future cash flows and pricing power

questions.explanation: The physical assets may remain, but expected future cash flows can drop sharply if trust erodes, regulators respond, or customers churn.

questions.stem: A student says: 'Book value equals firm value.' Which correction is best?

options.A: Book value captures customer satisfaction; market value reflects employee engagement only
options.B: Book value captures expectations; market value reflects only historical accounting costs
options.C: Book value captures share price; market value reflects depreciation schedules only
options.D: Book value captures historical costs; market value reflects future expectations and intangibles

questions.explanation: Balance sheets are backward looking and incomplete for intangibles. Markets capitalise expected future cash flows and risk, which often makes market diverge from book.

questions.stem: A student says: 'Market cap is cash the firm has.' Which correction is most accurate?

options.A: Market cap is the revenue multiple, so it equals annual sales times a constant factor
options.B: Market cap is the retained earnings total, so it equals cumulative accounting profit
options.C: Market cap is the market valuation of equity, not the cash balance on the balance sheet
options.D: Market cap is the accounting value of assets, so it equals cash plus inventory always

questions.explanation: Market cap equals share price times shares outstanding. It is a valuation, not a cash account, and it can move without any immediate balance-sheet cash change.

questions.stem: If market value falls while accounting profit is stable, what is the most disciplined first hypothesis?

options.A: Expectations about future cash flows worsened due to competition, disruption, or reputation risk
options.B: Accounting profit must be wrong because profit always determines price in the short run
options.C: Price cannot move without dividends, so the market value must be a reporting error
options.D: Book value must have changed because market equals book for all firms in equilibrium

questions.explanation: Markets are forward looking. A stable current profit can coexist with a lower valuation if investors expect future margins, growth, or stability to decline.

questions.stem: In efficient market framing, share price most directly reflects what?

options.A: Aggregated expectations based on available information about future cash flows and risk
options.B: The firms CSR announcements independent of product performance and competitive dynamics
options.C: The firms book value independent of growth expectations and discount rates
options.D: The CEOs moral integrity independent of any financial expectations or operating data

questions.explanation: In EMH-style reasoning, prices incorporate publicly available information. They therefore reflect expected cash flows discounted for risk, not only past accounting performance.

questions.stem: Two firms have the same market cap, but Firm Y has much higher net debt than Firm X. In enterprise value terms, what is the most accurate implication?

options.A: Enterprise value is the same as book value, so leverage cannot affect it
options.B: Firm Y can have a higher enterprise value because EV adds net debt to equity value
options.C: Firm Y must have a lower enterprise value because debt is excluded from valuation
options.D: Both firms must have identical enterprise value because EV equals market cap by definition

questions.explanation: Enterprise value approximates the value of the operating business to all capital providers: EV = market value of equity + net debt (and other claims). Higher net debt can raise EV even if market cap is identical.

questions.stem: Which is the most common and most wrong inference about intangibles?

options.A: Patents are hard and therefore never strategic in platform and network markets
options.B: Factories are hard and therefore always strategic, even in commoditised categories
options.C: Brand is soft and therefore non-strategic, even though it can create pricing power
options.D: Inventory is soft and therefore always irrelevant to liquidity and solvency

questions.explanation: Intangibles can be causal. Brand trust can raise willingness to pay and retention, affecting the wedge as much as tangible assets affect cost.

questions.stem: Which measure is most likely a leading indicator of intangible strength in a consumer brand?

options.A: Inventory count, because inventory count is the same as loyalty and preference
options.B: Depreciation expense, because depreciation rises when brand equity rises
options.C: Total assets, because assets increase whenever brand trust increases automatically
options.D: Repeat purchase interval and low return rates paired with stable pricing power

questions.explanation: Leading indicators capture behaviour: retention, repeat, returns, and ability to hold price. These can precede changes in accounting profitability.

questions.stem: Which statement best connects intangible advantage to the economic wedge?

options.A: Intangibles matter only when they increase book value through capitalisation rules
options.B: Intangibles matter when they raise willingness to pay or lower cost relative to rivals
options.C: Intangibles matter only when they raise inventory levels because brand means stock
options.D: Intangibles matter only when they reduce taxes because reputation drives tax rates down

questions.explanation: The wedge is about value created and cost incurred. Intangibles are strategic when they shift those economics: pricing power, retention, adoption risk, or productivity.

questions.stem: Why can a scandal destroy value faster than it destroys accounting profit?

options.A: It forces dividends to become zero overnight because regulators prohibit distributions
options.B: It changes expectations about future cash flows immediately, while accounting updates with lag
options.C: It forces share count to double overnight because exchanges rebalance indexes instantly
options.D: It forces book value to become zero overnight because standards require full write offs

questions.explanation: Valuation is forward looking and can reprice instantly. Accounting profits may remain temporarily stable even as future growth and margins are expected to decline.

questions.stem: Why can accounting data understate advantage in intangible-heavy firms?

options.A: Accounting always capitalises brand equity, so advantage is typically overstated in reports
options.B: Accounting ignores revenue, so growth firms cannot report sales under standards
options.C: Many intangible investments like brand building and R&D are expensed rather than capitalised
options.D: Accounting ignores costs, so profitability always appears higher than economic reality

questions.explanation: Expenses can reduce reported profit even when they build long-run capability. This can make accounting statements look weaker than the firm's strategic position.

questions.stem: A CEO debate: allocate 1B profit to buybacks vs reinvestment in experience. Best scorecard way to decide?

options.A: Choose neither because scorecards avoid trade-offs by maximising all measures simultaneously
options.B: Choose buybacks because financial metrics dominate all other perspectives in strategy
options.C: Choose reinvestment because learning metrics dominate and financial outcomes are secondary
options.D: Test both paths on causal drivers and outcomes: capability, customer metrics, then financial results

questions.explanation: The scorecard is designed to connect investments to leading drivers and then to lagging outcomes. The decision should be guided by expected causal effects and evidence.

questions.stem: A circular initiative reduces waste but raises unit cost. When is it most defensible strategically?

options.A: When rivalry increases, because rivalry forces efficiency in all firms equally over time
options.B: When market value falls temporarily, because markets reward short-run pain automatically
options.C: When accounting cost rises, because higher reported costs always raise brand legitimacy
options.D: When willingness to pay or retention rises enough to widen V-C despite higher cost

questions.explanation: The wedge is the test: if value rises more than cost, the initiative can strengthen advantage. Otherwise, it may be ethically admirable but economically fragile.

questions.stem: A company publishes a glossy impact report but cannot show operating changes. The best diagnosis is:

options.A: Value chain productivity by definition, because storytelling reduces transaction costs permanently
options.B: Shared value by definition, because any impact report automatically improves competitive advantage
options.C: Cluster development by definition, because reporting implies local investment and supplier upgrading
options.D: A reputation narrative with weak causal pathway to competitiveness; shared value is unproven

questions.explanation: Without operational change or measurable links to cost, quality, productivity, or demand, claims remain rhetoric. Shared value requires evidence and mechanisms.

questions.stem: A firm adds more scorecard metrics every quarter. What is the best design caution?

options.A: More measures always improves trust because transparency automatically raises value
options.B: More measures always improves profitability because it increases accountability instantly
options.C: More measures always improves control because measurement is the same as execution
options.D: Too many measures can dilute focus; metrics should map to the causal strategy logic

questions.explanation: A scorecard should be selective. Measures must be tied to strategy and actionable; otherwise they become reporting noise rather than control tools.

questions.stem: A firm claims 'we are a purpose brand, so price does not matter.' Which response is most correct?

options.A: Price does not matter because regulations guarantee mission brands fixed profit margins
options.B: Price does not matter because customers ignore price when values are aligned sufficiently
options.C: Price does not matter because purpose brands always receive free capital and donations
options.D: Price still matters because capture determines whether the mission can fund itself sustainably

questions.explanation: Mission requires margin. Even value-creating strategies can fail if they cannot capture enough surplus to reinvest and remain solvent.

questions.stem: A firm claims shared value because it made a one-time donation unrelated to operations. The most accurate classification is:

options.A: Traditional CSR or philanthropy, because there is no operational link to competitiveness
options.B: Cluster development, because any donation automatically strengthens local supplier clusters
options.C: Shared value by definition, because social spending always improves competitive advantage
options.D: Value chain productivity, because any donation reduces transaction costs in the ecosystem

questions.explanation: Shared value requires a measurable link between social improvement and competitive performance. Pure donations can be valuable ethically, but they are not shared value.

questions.stem: A firm introduces circular resale but fails to price services well. What breaks first?

options.A: Market cap: it must rise automatically because circularity is always fashionable
options.B: Value capture: customers benefit, but producer surplus remains weak and profits stay thin
options.C: Consumer surplus: customers lose value even though services are free and convenient
options.D: Liquidity: ratios become undefined because services cannot be recorded in financial statements

questions.explanation: Circularity can create value while failing to capture it. Without pricing discipline, service margins remain low and the initiative cannot fund itself.

questions.stem: A firm reports rising donations but declining retention and rising returns. What is the best integrated scorecard diagnosis?

options.A: Donations reduce cost leadership pressure, so rising returns are a sign of growth
options.B: Customer and process drivers are failing; financial giving cannot substitute for product reliability
options.C: Donations eliminate substitutes, so retention can fall without harming long-run performance
options.D: Donations prove success; retention is irrelevant once moral positioning is strong enough

questions.explanation: In the scorecard logic, customer and internal process failures eventually harm financial outcomes. Philanthropy cannot compensate for weak product performance and service experience.

questions.stem: A firm says 'purpose eliminates trade-offs.' Which response is most accurate under this syllabus?

options.A: Purpose clarifies priorities, but trade-offs still exist in price, cost, and scope choices
options.B: Purpose eliminates trade-offs because customers always pay more for moral positioning
options.C: Purpose eliminates trade-offs because authenticity automatically lowers costs over time
options.D: Purpose eliminates trade-offs because regulation protects mission firms from rivalry

questions.explanation: Strategy remains a set of choices under constraints. Purpose can guide choices, but it does not remove economic scarcity or competitive trade-offs.

questions.stem: A firm uses ESG ratings as its only KPI. Which critique best fits this syllabus?

options.A: Ratings replace liquidity analysis; current and quick ratios are irrelevant to governance
options.B: Ratings can be noisy and lagging; wedge-linked drivers and operational measures are still needed
options.C: Ratings replace market prices; market cap cannot be used for performance evaluation at all
options.D: Ratings are perfect; wedge and accounting measures become redundant once ratings are high

questions.explanation: External ratings can help, but they can differ across providers and may lag operational reality. Strategy needs internal leading indicators tied to value creation and capture.

questions.stem: A manager says 'Balanced Scorecard means we maximise every metric.' Which correction is best?

options.A: Scorecard removes trade-offs, because multiple objectives can be maximised simultaneously
options.B: Scorecard aligns trade-offs to strategy; some metrics are drivers and others are constraints
options.C: Scorecard replaces strategy, because the choice of metrics is the strategy itself
options.D: Scorecard is only for nonprofits, so firms should track financials only

questions.explanation: The scorecard is a strategy execution system. It clarifies causal links and priorities rather than pretending all objectives can be maximised at once.

questions.stem: A recession hits; a mission firm switches to cheaper materials for one year. Which reasoning is most conceptually correct?

options.A: Short-run cost falls, so substitutes disappear because rivals cannot match cost reductions
options.B: Short-run cost may fall, but credibility loss can reduce value more than the savings
options.C: Short-run cost falls, so value must rise because customers reward cost discipline always
options.D: Short-run cost falls, so accounting profit proves wedge expands automatically and sustainably

questions.explanation: If credibility is a core intangible, compromising it can shrink willingness to pay and retention. The wedge can therefore narrow even if accounting costs temporarily fall.

questions.stem: A scorecard includes only lagging outcomes like revenue and profit. What is the deepest design flaw?

options.A: It becomes too moral because lagging outcomes are ethically biased measures
options.B: It cannot guide action because leading drivers and causal links are missing
options.C: It becomes too complex because lagging measures require excessive data collection
options.D: It becomes too financial because lagging outcomes are only for accountants

questions.explanation: Lagging measures tell you what happened, not what to do. The scorecard works by linking leading drivers (process, capability) to outcomes.

questions.stem: A scorecard shows customer metrics improving while internal process metrics worsen. Best disciplined interpretation?

options.A: Customer metrics prove execution is strong, so internal metrics can be ignored safely
options.B: Internal metrics prove monopoly, so customer outcomes cannot matter in market performance
options.C: Internal metrics prove liquidity, so customer metrics are just soft signals and irrelevant
options.D: A short-run demand lift may be unsustainable if execution capability and process discipline erode

questions.explanation: Customer outcomes can improve temporarily through promotions or messaging. If processes deteriorate, quality and cost can worsen later, harming sustainability.

questions.stem: A startup says it creates shared value because it employs people. Best correction?

options.A: Employment is shared value only when it reduces market value temporarily to fund expansion
options.B: Employment alone is not shared value; it must measurably improve competitiveness and social outcomes
options.C: Employment is shared value only when it increases buybacks and dividends for owners
options.D: Employment is always shared value; competitiveness is irrelevant to the definition by design

questions.explanation: Shared value requires an integrated business case. Employment can be part of it, but the link to productivity, product value, or cluster strength must be demonstrated.

questions.stem: In a Balanced Scorecard, '100 percent traceable supply chain' belongs primarily to which perspective?

options.A: Customer, because it directly measures willingness to pay and perceived brand meaning
options.B: Internal process, because it reflects how the firm creates value and controls execution
options.C: Financial, because it directly measures profit, cash flow, and shareholder returns
options.D: Learning and growth, because it directly measures employee skills and retention levels

questions.explanation: Traceability is an internal capability and process metric. It is a driver that supports customer trust and financial outcomes, not a direct financial result.

questions.stem: In the Balanced Scorecard, 'employee retention above 95 percent' is best classified as:

options.A: Financial, because retention is the same as ROE and cash flow performance
options.B: Learning and growth, because it indicates capability accumulation and cultural stability
options.C: Internal process, because retention is a direct measure of supply chain cycle time
options.D: Customer, because retention directly measures customer willingness to pay and loyalty

questions.explanation: High retention supports learning, culture, and operational consistency. It is a leading indicator that can improve execution quality and customer outcomes later.

questions.stem: In the scorecard, 'Ironclad Guarantee returns below 2 percent' fits best as:

options.A: Financial perspective, because it directly measures dividend yield and shareholder value
options.B: Learning perspective, because it directly measures training hours and skill acquisition
options.C: Internal process perspective, because it directly measures cycle time and traceability
options.D: Customer perspective, because it reflects perceived quality and trust for buyers

questions.explanation: Low returns are experienced by customers as reliability and reduced hassle. It is a customer-facing outcome that can drive loyalty and willingness to pay.

questions.stem: Patagonia pays a 1 percent of sales 'Earth tax'. In scorecard terms, the best classification is:

options.A: Customer perspective, because it directly measures customer satisfaction and willingness to pay
options.B: Learning perspective, because it directly measures training hours and talent development
options.C: Financial perspective, because it is a resource allocation rule tied to revenue and reinvestment choices
options.D: Internal perspective, because it directly measures traceability and cycle time performance

questions.explanation: The Earth tax is a financial commitment. It does not directly measure customer perceptions or internal processes, but it can support credibility and mission over time.

questions.stem: Which example best fits 'redefine value chain productivity' as shared value?

options.A: Donating to climate causes after profits, regardless of whether operations change
options.B: Reducing energy per unit compute while maintaining performance, lowering cost and emissions together
options.C: Lobbying for weaker emissions rules to reduce compliance costs without innovation
options.D: Publishing sustainability pages while keeping the same supply chain practices

questions.explanation: Productivity improvements that reduce environmental impact and cost simultaneously are classic shared value. They strengthen competitiveness while improving social outcomes.

questions.stem: Which is the most rigorous test of whether 'purpose' is creating competitive advantage?

options.A: Show that value rises or cost falls relative to rivals over time, with evidence in pricing and retention
options.B: Show that executives feel proud, because pride reliably predicts profitability and market value
options.C: Show that employees volunteer more hours, because volunteering is the same as productivity
options.D: Show that mission statements are shared more often on social media and press coverage grows

questions.explanation: Purpose becomes strategic when it changes the wedge: willingness to pay, retention, adoption risk, or productivity, relative to competitors.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest reason purpose can be strategically fragile?

options.A: If operationalised, it always raises cost and therefore always kills advantage
options.B: If operationalised, it eliminates substitutes because rivals cannot copy morals
options.C: If not operationalised, it becomes cheap talk and loses wedge relevance quickly
options.D: If not operationalised, it still raises value automatically because morality sells

questions.explanation: Purpose works when it is embedded in capabilities, governance, and product design. Otherwise it is easy to imitate and easy for stakeholders to doubt.

questions.stem: Which list correctly captures the three shared value routes?

options.A: Improve branding; hire influencers; issue purpose statements every quarter
options.B: Reconceive products and markets; redefine value chain productivity; enable local clusters
options.C: Reduce taxes; increase buybacks; lobby regulators for preferential rules
options.D: Donate profits; publish ESG reports; sponsor employee volunteering and pledges

questions.explanation: Shared value is about integrating social and competitive advantage through core business models, not add-on philanthropy or pure communication.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes an impact report from a strategy in this syllabus?

options.A: Reports explain mechanisms; strategy describes only what happened in the last quarter
options.B: Reports equal market cap; strategy equals book value, so both are accounting constructs
options.C: Reports equal liquidity; strategy equals quick ratio, so both are solvency tools
options.D: Reports describe outcomes; strategy explains mechanisms linking actions to wedge and performance

questions.explanation: A strategy needs a causal story and choices. Reporting can be useful, but without mechanisms it does not guide competitive action.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the Balanced Scorecard appears in the Patagonia module?

options.A: It proves purpose is sufficient; firms can ignore costs if mission is clear and strong
options.B: It replaces competitive analysis; firms can skip wedge logic if they use a scorecard
options.C: It is required by law; firms must use scorecards in annual reports and filings
options.D: It aligns mission, operational drivers, customer value, and financial outcomes in one system

questions.explanation: Patagonia is used to show how mission can be translated into measurable drivers and outcomes. The scorecard provides a structure for that translation.
